results.claim: THEOREM 3.10: the logarithmically averaged Chowla conjecture (all k) and the logarithmically averaged Sarnak conjecture are logically equivalent, and both are equivalent to the 'local Gowers uniformity' of lambda; plus the un-averaged Chowla conjecture implies the un-averaged Sarnak conjecture.
results.paper_quote: Abstract: "Our main result is that these latter two conjectures are logically equivalent to each other, as well as to the \"local Gowers uniformity\" of the Liouville function." Sec. 1: "Theorem 1.8. Conjectures 1.3, 1.4, 1.5, 1.6, 1.7 are equivalent." and "In [50] it was observed that Conjecture 1.2 was implied by Conjecture 1.1" (un-averaged Chowla implies Sarnak).
results.doc_quote: "The logarithmically averaged Chowla conjecture (all `k`) and the logarithmically averaged Sarnak conjecture are **logically equivalent**, and both are equivalent to the "local Gowers uniformity" of `λ`. Also, the **un-averaged** Chowla conjecture implies the Sarnak conjecture."
results.notes: Read in full at arxiv.org/html/1605.04628v1 (abs page also read: single version, v1, 16 May 2016, so no version or numbering drift). Archive's "THEOREM 3.10" is its own dictionary-ledger number; the paper's numbered result is Theorem 1.8. "local Gowers uniformity" = Conjecture 1.6 (with constraint 2<=H<=omega<=X); log-Sarnak = Conjecture 1.5 for deterministic f (zero topological entropy). Archive correctly keeps the averaged/un-averaged distinction; both abstract quotes are verbatim; the Chowla=>Sarnak implication is attributed by the paper to Sarnak [50], not proved there.

results.claim: The k=1 case of the Chowla conjecture, sum_{n<=x} lambda(n) = o(x), is equivalent to the prime number theorem and is therefore a theorem, not open; quoted to Tao arXiv:1605.04628 Sec. 1.
results.paper_quote: Sec. 1 (Introduction), unnumbered prose, p. 2: "The $k=1$ case of the Chowla conjecture is equivalent to the prime number theorem. The higher $k$ cases are open, although there are a number of partial results available if one allows for some averaging in the $b_{1},\dots,b_{k}$ parameters..."
results.doc_quote: *"The `k=1` case of the Chowla conjecture is equivalent to the prime number theorem. The higher `k` cases are open."*
results.notes: Quote check: first sentence verbatim; the second sentence is truncated at "open" and the paper's comma becomes a period (paper continues ", although there are a number of partial results available ..."). The quoted words are exact, so truncation, not misquotation. It is unnumbered prose in Sec. 1, not a numbered theorem. Conjecture 1.1 states the k=1 case as sum lambda(a_1 n+b_1)=o(X) for fixed a_1 in N, b_1>=0; the doc's sum lambda(n)=o(x) is the a_1=1,b_1=0 instance. The paper calls lambda(n)=sum_{d^2|n} mu(n/d^2) "a routine application"; the doc's attribution of lambda=1_squares*mu to Landau is not in the paper but does not conflict.

results.claim: Correction row X1: the round's claim that one-point Chowla sum_{n<=x} lambda(n) = o(x) is OPEN is false; it is equivalent to PNT, i.e. a theorem, via lambda = 1_squares * mu giving sum_{n<=x} lambda(n) = sum_{d<=sqrt(x)} M(x/d^2) = o(x) from M(y) = o(y); cited to Tao arXiv:1605.04628 (with MRT arXiv:1509.01545).
results.paper_quote: Sec. 1: "The $k=1$ case of the Chowla conjecture is equivalent to the prime number theorem." and, in the same paragraph, "A routine application of the identity $\mu(n)=\sum_{d^{2}|n}\mu(d)\lambda(\frac{n}{d^{2}})$ (or the inverse identity $\lambda(n)=\sum_{d^{2}|n}\mu(\frac{n}{d^{2}})$)...".
results.doc_quote: | X1 | "one-point Chowla `Σ_{n≤x}λ(n) = o(x)` is itself **OPEN**" (rh46 §1.3, rh47 §5.1) | **false** — it is **equivalent to PNT**, i.e. a **theorem**.  `λ = 1_squares ∗ μ`, so `Σ_{n≤x}λ(n) = Σ_{d≤√x} M(x/d²) = o(x)` follows from `M(y) = o(y)` |
results.notes: The uncited secondary reference checks out too: Matomaki-Radziwill-Tao arXiv:1509.01545v2 Sec. 1 (Conjecture 1.3 and the line after it) reads "For $k=1$, this claim is equivalent to the prime number theorem, but for $k>1$ Chowla's conjecture remains open." The paper's own identity lambda(n) = sum_{d^2|n} mu(n/d^2) is the doc's lambda = 1_squares * mu, and the displayed double-sum derivation is the standard one. Paper has only v1 (16 May 2016); neither archive doc cites a version, and none is needed. Claim is in both directions, as the paper states.
